title: The Gatekeepers
subtitle: Transplant access from the inside: referral, evaluation, the waiting list, organ procurement, discarded kidneys, and the innovation left waiting at the door
outcomes: Identify each gate between kidney failure and a transplant, and who controls it
Explain how waiting time is earned, how race-based equations cost Black patients years, and how that is being corrected
Interpret organ nonuse data and the evidence on machine perfusion
Describe how organ procurement organizations are measured and policed, including the October 2026 federal rule
Evaluate emerging tools, including perfusion, oxygen-carrier research such as BHOC, and xenotransplant trials, without overstating them

scenes.text: Welcome back. In Course 1 you saw the machine. In this course, we look at the way out of it. For most people with kidney failure, a transplant means a longer life and a better one than dialysis. But between a patient and a new kidney stand a series of gates. Each has a keeper. Most patients never learn who they are.

v.sub: Referral: the first gate, and the most often locked

scenes.text: Here are the gates, in order. Someone has to refer you. A transplant center has to accept the referral and evaluate you. You have to be listed. Time has to pass while you accumulate waiting time. An organ has to be recovered, offered, and accepted. And then the surgery has to happen. Any one of those gates can quietly close.

v.title: The gates to a transplant
v.note: Each gate has a different keeper: dialysis facility, nephrologist, transplant center, OPTN policy, organ procurement organization, surgical team.

scenes.text: The first gate is referral, and it is mostly kept by the dialysis facility and the nephrologist. Federal rules do speak to it. Every Medicare dialysis facility must evaluate each patient's suitability for a transplant referral. If the team decides a patient is not suitable, the reason must be documented in the medical record. And the facility must track every referral it sends. Yet in the Georgia study you saw in Course 1, the median facility referred only about one in four patients within a year.

v.h: What federal rules require on transplant referral
items: Evaluate every patient's suitability for a transplant referral
If not suitable: document the basis for nonreferral in the medical record
Track the results of each transplant center referral
Communicate with the transplant center about status at least annually
v.src: Code of Federal Regulations, Title 42, Part 494

scenes.text: Timing matters enormously. A transplant before dialysis, called preemptive, is the best outcome for many patients. In 2024, about thirty-two percent of adults who received a kidney from a living donor had never needed dialysis. For people who received a kidney from a deceased donor, it was fifteen percent. Early referral and an engaged donor make the difference.

items: Had no prior dialysis, 2024
Had no prior dialysis, 2024

scenes.prompt: Your brother has been on dialysis for eight months. No one has mentioned a transplant. What's the strongest next step?

options.t: Wait for the care team to bring it up
options.fb: In many facilities that conversation never starts on its own. Waiting is the most common way patients lose years.

options.t: Call a transplant center directly and ask whether he can self-refer, while asking his nephrologist in writing to send a referral
options.fb: Right. Many centers accept self-referrals, and a written request to the nephrologist creates a record. Doing both closes the gate from two sides.

options.t: Assume he isn't a candidate because of his age or health
options.fb: Only a transplant center's evaluation can decide candidacy. Never let anyone screen a patient out by assumption.

scenes.text: Here's something many people don't realize. Your waiting time for a deceased-donor kidney is counted from either the day you started dialysis or the day you were listed with a filtration rate of twenty or below, whichever came first. So for someone already on dialysis, a late referral doesn't erase all their waiting time. But it does delay the evaluation, the listing, and every living-donor conversation that could have happened sooner.

v.text: Waiting time can be credited back to the dialysis start date. Evaluation time cannot. Every month of delayed referral is a month the rest of the process didn't move.

scenes.text: Your tool for this gate: ask the dialysis social worker, in writing, three things. Has a transplant referral been sent, and to which center? On what date? And what did the center say? If no referral was sent, ask to see the documented reason. Federal rules require the facility to write it down. A missing reason is itself something you can raise.

v.title: Opening the first gate
items: Has a referral been sent? To which center?
On what date, and what did the center reply?
If not referred: ask for the documented basis for nonreferral (42 CFR 494.80(a)(10))
Ask transplant centers about self-referral directly

quiz.q: Who most often controls the first gate, referral for transplant?
quiz.why: Referral usually comes from the nephrologist and dialysis team, and rates vary enormously by facility.

quiz.q: If a dialysis team decides a patient is not suitable for transplant referral, what do federal rules require?
o: The basis for nonreferral must be documented in the medical record
quiz.why: 42 CFR 494.80(a)(10) requires an evaluation of suitability for referral and documentation of the basis for nonreferral.

quiz.q: In 2024, what share of adult living-donor kidney recipients had never needed dialysis?
quiz.why: 31.8%, versus 15.0% for deceased-donor recipients (SRTR 2024).

quiz.q: From when is deceased-donor waiting time generally counted?
o: The date of the first clinic visit
The dialysis start date, or listing with eGFR of 20 or below, whichever is earlier
Only from the date of listing, no exceptions
quiz.why: This is why waiting time can be credited back to the dialysis start, but delayed evaluation still costs time.

scenes.text: Getting referred is not getting listed. The second gate is the transplant evaluation, and it is run entirely by the transplant center. Each center sets much of its own selection criteria. Two centers in the same city can look at the same patient and reach different answers.

v.sub: Where medical judgment and quiet gatekeeping meet

scenes.text: A typical evaluation includes heart testing, cancer screening, dental clearance, blood work, imaging, meetings with a surgeon, a nephrologist, a social worker, a financial counselor, and often a dietitian and a pharmacist. Each one is a separate appointment, often on a separate day, often far from home.

v.title: A typical evaluation
items: Cardiac testing
Cancer screenings
Dental clearance
Labs and imaging
Surgeon, nephrologist, social worker
Financial counseling
Dietitian, pharmacist

scenes.text: Some requirements are clearly medical. Others are not. Many programs require a named support person, a care partner who commits to transportation and help after surgery. Many require proof that the patient can afford anti-rejection medications. Some use body-weight cutoffs. These rules can be reasonable. They also fall hardest on people without money, a car, or family nearby.

items: Heart and cancer screening
Infection risk
Surgical fitness
Required support person
Proof of medication coverage
Transportation
Some center-specific cutoffs

scenes.text: In 2022, the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine called the U.S. transplant system demonstrably inequitable. They found that people of color and people with disabilities are disadvantaged in access, referral and waiting time. Among their recommendations: more transparency, and better communication between transplant teams and the people waiting.

v.text: The U.S. organ transplant system is demonstrably inequitable.
v.by: National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, Realizing the Promise of Equity in the Organ Transplantation System, 2022

scenes.text: Some of that is starting to change. In May 2026, Medicare finalized changes to the IOTA transplant model that require participating hospitals to notify patients when their waiting list status changes. A proposed requirement to tell patients about organ offers the center declined on their behalf was not finalized. That second piece is worth pushing for.

items: Adopted: notify patients when waitlist status changes
Not finalized: notifying patients of organ offers declined on their behalf
Medicare Advantage patients now included in performance payments

scenes.prompt: Tap each card for a question to ask at the first evaluation visit.

cards.b: Please give me your selection criteria in writing, including any weight, age, or support-person rules.
What is your typical time from referral to listing? What would speed mine up?
If you don't list me, will you give me the reason in writing, and can I be evaluated elsewhere?
Will you tell me when you decline an organ offer for me, and why?
Can I be evaluated and listed at more than one center?

scenes.text: Remember that a center saying no is not the end. Patients can seek evaluation at another program, and in some cases be listed at more than one. A written reason for a decline is the single most valuable document an advocate can hold. It turns a closed door into a problem that can be solved, or challenged.

v.text: A decline without a written reason is a wall. A decline with a written reason is a to-do list.

quiz.q: Who runs the transplant evaluation and sets much of its selection criteria?
quiz.why: Criteria vary by center, which is why two centers can reach different answers about the same patient.

quiz.q: What did the National Academies conclude in 2022?
quiz.why: Realizing the Promise of Equity in the Organ Transplantation System (2022) called it demonstrably inequitable.

quiz.q: What did the May 2026 IOTA update require of participating hospitals?
o: Notifying patients of waitlist status changes
quiz.why: Waitlist status notifications were adopted; declined-offer notifications were not finalized.

quiz.q: What is the most valuable document after a transplant center declines a patient?
o: The written reason for the decline
quiz.why: A written reason lets you address the issue or seek evaluation elsewhere.

sources.t: National Academies: Realizing the Promise of Equity in the Organ Transplantation System (2022)

modules.title: The List: Time, Race, and the Rules

scenes.text: Now the list itself. In 2024, about one hundred and forty-four thousand adults were on the kidney waiting list at some point during the year. A record forty-nine thousand two hundred and forty-nine were newly added. About one in ten had been waiting five years or more.

items.label: adults on the kidney waiting list at any time in 2024

scenes.prompt: In 2024, how many adults were removed from the kidney waiting list because they had become TOO SICK to receive a transplant?
scenes.fb: 4,901 adults were removed as too sick in 2024, and another 3,743 were removed because they died (SRTR 2024). Together, more than 8,600 people left the list without a transplant.

scenes.text: Four thousand nine hundred and one people were removed as too sick, and three thousand seven hundred and forty-three were removed because they died. Combined, more than eight thousand six hundred people left the list in one year without the kidney they were waiting for. Every number on this slide was a person with a care partner who did everything they were told.

v.title: Left the adult kidney waiting list without a transplant, 2024

scenes.text: For decades, the most common formula for estimating kidney function included a multiplier for Black patients. It made their kidneys look healthier than they were. Because waiting time can start at a filtration rate of twenty or below, that formula delayed when Black patients could start earning time on the list.

v.text: A race multiplier made Black patients' kidney function appear higher, which delayed the point at which they could begin earning waiting time.

scenes.text: In July 2022, the national transplant network required race-neutral formulas. In January 2023, it went further: every transplant program had to review its Black candidates and give back the waiting time they had lost, with a deadline of January 2024. By July 2023, more than six thousand one hundred Black candidates had their time modified, with a median of one point seven years restored. Within a year of the policy, the network reported more than fourteen thousand seven hundred modifications.

items.t: Programs must identify and restore lost waiting time

scenes.text: That correction happened because patients, physicians and advocates documented the harm and kept pushing. It is one of the clearest recent examples of advocacy changing a national rule. If you or someone you help is Black and was waitlisted before 2023, confirm in writing that the waiting time review was done.

v.title: Advocate's check
items: Black candidate listed before 2023?
Ask the program in writing: was a waiting time review completed?
If modified: how much time was restored, and from what date?
Keep the answer in your care file

scenes.prompt: A patient's waiting time looks shorter than her dialysis history suggests. What should you ask first?

options.t: Whether her waiting time was counted from her dialysis start date
options.fb: Right. Waiting time generally counts from the dialysis start or qualifying eGFR listing, whichever is earlier. A mismatch is worth a written question.

options.t: Whether she can pay to move up
options.fb: Organ allocation cannot be bought. Federal law prohibits buying or selling organs.

options.t: Nothing; the list is always right
options.fb: Lists are kept by people and software. Errors and policy changes happen. Verify.

quiz.q: In 2024, about how many adults were removed from the kidney list as too sick to transplant?
quiz.why: 4,901 as too sick, plus 3,743 removed due to death (SRTR 2024).

quiz.q: Why did race-inclusive kidney function formulas harm Black candidates?
o: They made kidney function look higher, delaying when waiting time could begin
quiz.why: The multiplier inflated estimated function, delaying the eGFR-of-20 threshold.

quiz.q: What was the median waiting time restored in early monitoring of the 2023 policy?
quiz.why: Median 1.7 years among the first 6,103 modifications (HRSA/OPTN).

sources.t: OPTN/SRTR 2024 Annual Data Report: Kidney
HRSA/OPTN: Early monitoring of waiting time modifications
OPTN: Waiting time modifications (a closer look)

scenes.text: This module is about the most painful number in the transplant system. A family says yes to donation. Surgeons recover the kidneys. And then a large share of them are never transplanted into anyone.

v.sub: Organ nonuse, and why it keeps rising

scenes.prompt: In 2024, what share of deceased-donor kidneys that were RECOVERED for transplant were never used?
scenes.fb: 29.3% in 2024, up from 18.2% in 2013 (OPTN/SRTR 2024). The report calls it a notable high.

scenes.text: Twenty-nine point three percent. Nearly three in ten kidneys recovered from deceased donors in 2024 were not used. In 2013, it was about eighteen percent. The trend is going the wrong way, while more than eight thousand people a year leave the list without a kidney.

v.label: About 29 of every 100 recovered deceased-donor kidneys went unused in 2024

scenes.text: Which kidneys go unused? Mostly those from older donors, those that were biopsied, and those with a high kidney donor profile score, meaning a statistically shorter expected life. Nonuse rates for those groups ran between forty and seventy percent. But a kidney with a shorter expected life can still mean years off dialysis for the right recipient, especially an older one.

In 2022 the National Academies set a goal: reduce kidney nonuse to five percent or less, and reach fifty thousand organs transplanted a year by 2026. In 2025 the country performed more than forty-nine thousand transplants of all organs, according to Medicare. Close on volume. Nowhere near the goal on waste.

items: Kidney nonuse target (2022)
Kidney nonuse rate

scenes.text: Why does it happen? Kidneys travel against a clock. Every hour on ice adds damage, called cold ischemia, the name of this foundation. Offers come at night. Operating rooms are booked. Centers worry about how a lower-quality kidney will affect their outcome statistics. And biopsy readings done in a hurry, on a frozen sample, can be unreliable.

v.title: Why a recovered kidney goes unused
steps: Offered down a list, often at night
Center weighs risk to its statistics

scenes.text: There is a better way to keep a kidney than ice alone. Hypothermic machine perfusion pumps a cold solution through the kidney while it waits. In a randomized trial published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2009, with three hundred and thirty-six donor kidney pairs, machine perfusion reduced delayed graft function from about twenty-six and a half percent to about twenty-one percent, and improved one-year kidney survival from ninety to ninety-four percent.

v.title: Machine perfusion vs. cold storage (NEJM 2009, 336 kidney pairs)
v.src: Moers et al., N Engl J Med 2009;360:7-19

scenes.text: That evidence is more than fifteen years old. Ask a transplant center how often it uses machine perfusion, and whether it will accept kidneys that other centers declined. Those two answers tell you a lot about how hard a program is willing to work to get a patient transplanted.

v.title: Two questions that reveal a program's posture
items: How often do you use machine perfusion?
Do you accept kidneys other centers have declined, for patients who want them?

quiz.q: What was the deceased-donor kidney nonuse rate in 2024?
What goal did the National Academies set for kidney nonuse?
quiz.why: 5% or less, plus 50,000 organs transplanted annually by 2026.

quiz.q: In the 2009 NEJM trial, how did machine perfusion affect delayed graft function?
o: Reduced it from about 26.5% to about 20.8%
quiz.why: Adjusted odds ratio 0.57; one-year graft survival 94% vs 90%.

quiz.q: What is cold ischemia?
o: Damage that accumulates while an organ is cold and without blood flow
quiz.why: Every hour on ice adds injury; reducing it is central to using more kidneys.

sources.t: OPTN/SRTR 2024 Annual Data Report: Kidney
Moers et al., Machine Perfusion or Cold Storage in Deceased-Donor Kidney Transplantation, NEJM 2009
National Academies report news release (2022)
CMS: OPO final rule press release (Oct 30, 2026)

scenes.text: Every donated organ in this country passes through one of fifty-some organ procurement organizations, called OPOs. Each holds a federal monopoly over its area. For decades they largely graded themselves. That has been changing, and in the last three years it has changed fast.

In November 2020, Medicare issued a rule that measures every OPO on two outcomes: how many donors it achieves, and how many organs it gets transplanted, both against the same count of potential donors in its area. OPOs are ranked into three tiers. The bottom tier, below the median on either measure, faces decertification, with full enforcement in 2026.

items.t: Above median, not top 25%: must compete for its area
Below median on either measure: decertified

scenes.text: In July 2025, federal regulators released findings that shook the public's trust. Reviewing three hundred and fifty-one cases at the OPO serving Kentucky, southwest Ohio and part of West Virginia, where donation was authorized but not completed, they found one hundred and three with concerning features, including seventy-three patients with neurological signs incompatible with donation. They concluded at least twenty-eight patients may not have been deceased when organ procurement was initiated.

items.label: showed neurological signs incompatible with donation
may not have been deceased when procurement began

scenes.text: The government ordered that OPO to complete a root cause analysis, create enforceable donor eligibility policies, and allow any staff member to halt a donation over safety concerns, under threat of decertification. Nationally, safety-related stoppages must now be reported to regulators. This matters to patients waiting for a kidney too. A system that loses public trust loses donors.

v.title: Reforms ordered, July 2025
items: Root cause analysis at the OPO, including failure to follow its own protocols
Enforceable donor eligibility policies
Any staff member may halt a donation over safety concerns
Safety-related stoppages reported to regulators nationwide
Accurate, complete information for families and hospitals

scenes.text: Then, on October 30, 2026, three weeks before this course was published, Medicare finalized another OPO rule. It defines unsound medical practices so the agency can decertify an OPO immediately, sets clearer rules for investigating adverse events, requires tracking of organs sent for research, lets high-performing OPOs compete for more areas, and requires orderly transitions when an OPO is replaced.

items: Defines 'unsound medical practices', enabling immediate decertification
Clearer adverse-event investigation and prevention
Organs sent for research must be tracked
Research-only pancreata no longer count toward transplant rate
High performers may compete for multiple areas; transition plans required

scenes.text: Medicare says that since its 2020 rule, organ donation has risen thirty-six percent and transplants thirty percent nationwide. Those are the agency's own figures, and worth noting as such. The lesson for an advocate is clear either way: measurement plus consequences changed behavior that decades of voluntary improvement did not.

items: Since the 2020 rule, per CMS
Since the 2020 rule, per CMS

scenes.prompt: Put these events in the order they happened.
items: CMS sets OPO outcome measures and tiers (Nov 2020)
Race-neutral kidney function formulas required (Jul 2022)
Federal findings on the Kentucky-region OPO (Jul 2025)
IOTA transplant model begins (Jul 2025)
CMS final rule on unsound practices and OPO competition (Oct 2026)
scenes.fb: Notice the pace: most of the structural change in this system happened in the last six years, much of it after sustained public pressure.

quiz.q: Under the 2020 rule, what happens to an OPO in Tier 3?
quiz.why: Tier 3 (below the median on either measure) faces decertification, with full enforcement in 2026.

quiz.q: In the July 2025 federal findings, how many patients may not have been deceased when procurement was initiated?
quiz.why: At least 28 of 351 cases reviewed (HHS, July 21, 2025).

quiz.q: What did the October 30, 2026 CMS rule do?
o: Defined unsound medical practices enabling immediate decertification, among other changes
quiz.why: It also tightened adverse-event rules, research-organ tracking, and transitions between OPOs.

scenes.text: Before we look at innovation, one more gate, and it's the most important. The best transplant most patients can get is a kidney from a living donor. Living-donor kidneys tend to last longer, the surgery can be scheduled, and many recipients never need dialysis at all. Yet this is the gate where the gap between who needs a kidney and who gets one is widest.

v.sub: The best option most patients have, and the hardest to reach

scenes.text: In 2024, there were six thousand four hundred and nineteen living-donor kidney transplants in the United States. That's up from about five thousand two hundred in 2020, but still below the peak of six thousand eight hundred and sixty-seven in 2019. Against a waiting list of about a hundred and forty-four thousand adults, living donation reaches only a sliver of the people who need it.

And it does not reach everyone equally. Black patients were about thirty-one percent of the adult waiting list in 2024, and thirteen percent of living-donor recipients. White patients were thirty-five percent of the list, and sixty percent of living-donor recipients. That gap is not about biology. It's about who in a patient's circle can afford to take weeks off work, who has paid leave, who has insurance, and who was ever asked.

v.title: Share of waiting list vs. share of living-donor recipients, 2024

scenes.text: The biggest single barrier is the ask. Most patients find it nearly impossible to ask someone for a kidney. Some programs train a friend or family member as a living donor champion, someone who tells the patient's story and spreads the word on their behalf, so the patient doesn't have to make the ask alone. If your transplant center has no such program, ask why.

v.text: Patients rarely ask for a kidney. A trained living donor champion can ask for them. Ask your center whether it supports one.

scenes.text: Compatibility is no longer the wall it once was. If a willing donor doesn't match their intended recipient, paired exchange programs can swap donors between pairs, sometimes in long chains, so that every recipient gets a compatible kidney. A mismatch is a reason to ask about paired exchange, not a reason to give up.

v.title: How a paired exchange works
steps: Donor A can't give to Recipient A
Donor B can't give to Recipient B
Donor A gives to Recipient B
Donor B gives to Recipient A

scenes.text: Then money. Federal law, the National Organ Transplant Act, forbids buying or selling organs. But donors can be reimbursed for real costs. The National Living Donor Assistance Center helps with them, and a 2020 federal rule allowed reimbursement of lost wages and dependent care. Since a change effective in late September 2026, eligibility is based on the donor's own income, not the recipient's. Donors up to five hundred percent of the federal poverty guidelines qualify; those between five and seven hundred fifty percent may qualify with a hardship waiver.

v.title: Living Donor Assistance eligibility (donor's income, % of federal poverty guidelines)
v.src: National Living Donor Assistance Center (2026 guidelines)

scenes.prompt: A friend says she might donate a kidney, but she can't afford two weeks without pay. What do you tell her?

options.t: Donation is unpaid, so she shouldn't do it
options.fb: Organs can't be bought, but donors can be reimbursed for real costs. Don't close the door for her.

options.t: Look into the National Living Donor Assistance Center, which can help with costs and, under a 2020 rule, lost wages and dependent care
options.fb: Right. Eligibility now depends on the donor's own income, and the transplant center's living donor coordinator can help apply.

options.t: Ask the recipient to pay her privately
options.fb: Paying for an organ is a federal crime under the National Organ Transplant Act. Legitimate reimbursement programs exist instead.

scenes.text: Your checklist for this gate: ask the transplant center whether it supports living donor champions, whether it participates in paired exchange, who its living donor coordinator is, and how it helps donors apply for financial assistance. A program that has crisp answers to all four is a program that is trying.

v.title: Four questions about living donation
items: Do you train or support living donor champions?
Do you participate in paired exchange?
Who is your living donor coordinator?
How do you help donors apply for financial assistance?

quiz.q: How many living-donor kidney transplants were performed in the U.S. in 2024?
quiz.why: 6,419, below the 2019 peak of 6,867 (SRTR 2024).

quiz.q: In 2024, Black patients were 30.5% of the adult waiting list. What share of living-donor recipients were Black?
quiz.why: 13.0%, while White patients were 59.9% of living-donor recipients.

quiz.q: A willing donor isn't compatible with their intended recipient. What should they ask about?
quiz.why: Paired exchange swaps donors between pairs so each recipient gets a compatible kidney.

quiz.q: Under the current NLDAC guidelines, whose income determines eligibility?
quiz.why: Since the September 2026 change, the donor's own income determines eligibility.

scenes.text: The last gate is the one nobody admits exists: the gate that keeps new ideas out. Kidney care in America has changed remarkably little in fifty years. The dialysis chair of 1975 would be familiar to a patient today. That is not because no one has better ideas. It is because the system pays for what already exists.

v.sub: Perfusion, oxygen carriers, xenotransplant, and living donation

scenes.text: Start with what's proven. Machine perfusion has randomized trial evidence going back to 2009. Researchers are now testing warm, or normothermic, perfusion that keeps an organ closer to body conditions, and can let teams assess it before transplant. These tools could help turn some of the twenty-nine percent of unused kidneys into transplants.

items: Organ on ice
Damage accumulates with time
Hard to assess before transplant
Solution pumped through the organ
Less delayed function in trials
Warm versions allow assessment

scenes.text: Then there's a question almost no patient has heard asked: what if a waiting organ could be given oxygen, not only cold? That is the research question behind oxygen carriers, including Biological Hemoglobin Oxygen Carriers, or BHOC, developed by BHOC Therapeutics. BHOC is a cell-free hemoglobin designed to carry oxygen and release it where tissue needs it, and designed to be compatible with all blood types.

items: Cell-free hemoglobin, with no red-cell antigens
Designed to be compatible with all blood types
Engineered oxygen affinity for controlled loading and release
A complementary oxygen-delivery bridge, not a replacement for blood
v.src: BHOC Therapeutics, as summarized on coldischemia.foundation/bhoc.html

scenes.text: Be precise about what that means. BHOC Therapeutics lists organ transplantation as one of its research areas, and maintains an evidence map of published research on oxygen carriers across the transplant journey. These are areas of research and development, not approved therapeutic claims. An honest advocate asks for that research to be funded and tested, and never claims results it hasn't produced.

v.text: Research areas, not approved claims. The advocate's job is to demand that promising research gets tested, and to describe it no further than the evidence goes.

scenes.text: And at the edge of the field: in February 2025, the FDA allowed the first formal clinical trial of kidneys from gene-edited pigs. Whether that becomes routine care is years away. But it shows that the supply of organs is not a fixed law of nature. It is a problem science and policy can work on, when someone insists.

v.title: Tools at or near the door

items.t: Randomized evidence for hypothermic machine perfusion
Normothermic perfusion in research and early use
Oxygen carriers such as BHOC studied across transplantation
FDA allows first formal pig-kidney xenotransplant trial

scenes.text: That's the gate system. Referral, evaluation, the list, procurement, nonuse, living donation, and innovation. Each one has a keeper, and each one can be pushed. In Course 3, we stop describing the system and start changing it. You'll learn your rights in writing, the escalation ladder, how to use evidence, and how rules actually get made.

quiz.q: How should an advocate describe BHOC accurately?
o: A cell-free hemoglobin oxygen carrier whose transplant uses are areas of research, not approved claims
A proven cure for organ damage
quiz.why: BHOC Therapeutics describes transplantation as a research area; it is not a replacement for blood or an approved therapy for that use.

quiz.q: What did the FDA allow in February 2025?
o: The first formal clinical trial of gene-edited pig kidneys
quiz.why: The first formal xenotransplant kidney trial.
